candidates.statement: This guidance introduces the concept of the individualized feature space 12 (IFS), which describes 93 the allowable limits of variation for the GE components of an individualized GE product. For 94 example, for a GE product whose only variable feature is a gRNA spacer sequence, the IFS 95 should describe which types of spacer sequences are allowable in the BLA – such as any spacer 96 sequence that targets a defined class of pathogenic gene variants in a specified gene and results 97 in the same editing outcome (e.g., correcting the gene so that it encodes the wild-type protein). A 98 new product variant should be considered a manufacturing change for purposes of the BLA – 99 rather than a new product – provided that: (1) the variable features of the product variant’s GE 100 components fall within the established IFS; and (2) the resulting product variant is predicted to 101 have adequate safety and activity based on clinical and/or in vitro data. Section III describes the 102 IFS in detail and provides additional examples of how it applies to individualized GE products. 103
candidates.context: 11 For the purposes of this guidance, a variable feature is defined as a physical characteristic of a genome editing component that differs from lot to lot, within defined limits, to address specific gene variants. III. THE INDIVIDUALIZED FEATURE SPACE 106

candidates.statement: 12 For the purposes of this guidance, an individualized feature space (IFS) is defined as the allowable limits of variation for one or more variable features of a product’s genome editing components. An IFS includes only features or combinations of features known or predicted to have adequate safety and activity. Adding a new product variant within a pre-defined IFS should not be considered to result in a new product.

candidates.statement: During process design, applicants define the commercial manufacturing process based on 218 knowledge gained through development and scale-up activities. For individualized GE 219 products, the goal is to design a process capable of reliably manufacturing all current and 220 future product variants that fall within the established IFS. In doing so, applicants should 221 distinguish between the IFS, which describes the allowable variable features of the GE 222 components, and the design space, 13 which describes the allowable limits for input 223 variables and process parameters in the manufacturing process. 224
candidates.context: A. Manufacturing Process Design and Control 216 Applicants should use process development studies and formal risk assessments 14 to 226 evaluate how the variable features of the GE components influence critical quality 227 attributes and critical process parameters. To avoid the need to revalidate the 228 manufacturing processes for each new GE component and product variant, the processes 229 should be robust enough to accommodate variable features across the entire IFS. In 230 particular, applicants should consider how GE components across the full range of the 231 IFS might affect material attributes, manufacturing parameters, and product quality. 232

candidates.statement: Manufacturing controls should be sufficiently robust to accommodate the full range of 234 variable features within the IFS. Some of these controls will differ between in vivo and ex 235 vivo products. For in vivo RNA-based products (where manufacturing control is primarily 236 achieved through chemical/biochemical synthesis parameters), variations in RNA 237 sequence length, GC content, or secondary structure may affect in vitro transcription 238 yields or solid-phase synthesis efficiency. The process should be controlled to ensure 239 consistent yield regardless of the specific sequence. Furthermore, changes to a gRNA 240 spacer sequence may alter the impurity profile or chromatographic retention time, 241 potentially requiring dynamic control of chromatography parameters (e.g., elution 242 gradients) to ensure consistent removal of product-related impurities. For lipid 243 nanoparticle products that contain RNA, if the length or secondary structure of the RNA 244 varies, process controls around mixing rates, flow rates, and lipid-to-RNA ratios should 245 be sufficiently robust to ensure consistent encapsulation efficiency and particle size. 246

candidates.statement: • Identity: Identity testing confirms that the correct individualized DP is in the 267 final container. Under 21 CFR 610.14, lot release identity tests must be performed 268 on DP sampled from its final container after completion of labeling, and they 269 must be adequate to distinguish the product from all other products being 270 processed in the same facility. For in vivo individualized GE products, identity 271 testing should include confirmation of the variable features of the GE components 272 (e.g., sequencing to confirm the correct gRNA spacer sequence). For ex vivo 273 products, identity testing should confirm the specific intended genomic edit in the 274 cellular DP. In addition, manufacturers of ex vivo products should establish and 275 document procedures for maintaining chain of identity (labeling and tracking) that 276 link the cellular starting material collected from a specific patient to the DP 277 manufactured from that material, at every stage of the manufacturing process. 278

candidates.statement: Expectations for manufacturing process validation apply to individualized GE products as 292 they do for all other products. 17 For individualized GE products, however, applicants 293 should adapt the traditional process validation approach to accommodate product 294 variability. At each stage, including process design, an applicant should address how 295 variable features affect manufacturing performance. There are also considerable 296 opportunities to leverage process validation information across product variants in an 297 individualized GE product. 298

candidates.statement: Process performance qualification (PPQ) studies should be designed based on a risk 300 assessment, and PPQ for individualized GE products should account for how variable 301 features and variable manufacturing conditions could affect process performance and 302 product quality. If certain feature variations or manufacturing variables are identified as 303 posing a high risk to product quality or process performance, then those aspects should be 304 evaluated during the PPQ campaign. For example, batch size for an individualized GE 305 product may range from large scale (for product variants intended for patients with 306 relatively common gene variants) to small scale (for product variants intended for only 307 one patient). For such a product that may be manufactured at different scales, PPQ 308 studies should include representative runs that bracket the extremes of process scale. In 309 general, however, if FDA determines that data from the process design stage is adequate 310 to ensure process performance across all potential product variants and GE components 311 in the IFS and across the anticipated range of manufacturing conditions, it should not be 312 essential for the PPQ campaign to include all variable features in the IFS or all potential 313 manufacturing conditions. 314

candidates.statement: As for all gene therapy products, FDA recommends that the BLA for an individualized 329 GE product include a potency assurance strategy. 18 Lot release testing must include one 330 or more potency assays as part of the DP release specification. 19 Demonstration of 331 potency for each lot should include confirmation that the GE components achieved the 332 desired editing outcome at or above an acceptance criterion based on data from clinical 333 studies. The assay(s) should be capable of quantitatively assessing the specific 334 contribution of the variable features of the GE components to product potency. 335
candidates.context: A. Activity and Potency Assurance 327 • For in vivo individualized GE products, potency assays may warrant developing 337 cell lines that include sequences that match the gene variants targeted by the 338 product. With such cell lines, for example, potency can be measured by 339 transducing the cell with the product, sequencing the targeted site, and measuring 340 successful editing of the gene variant to the intended sequence. Consideration 341 should be given to how the cell lines can be modified to include additional gene 342 variants as new product variants are added to the IFS. 343

candidates.statement: As discussed in Section VI.A, FDA may approve the addition of product variants to the 352 BLA based on in vitro safety and activity studies of GE components that have been 353 manufactured by representative processes. The activity studies can potentially use the 354 same potency and/or activity assays discussed in this section. Applicants should establish 355 appropriate acceptance criteria for these assays during clinical development, based on 356 potency data from product lots demonstrated to be clinically effective. For GE 357 components and in vivo products, expressing activity or potency as a relative value 358 against a thoroughly characterized reference material can facilitate the establishment of 359 meaningful acceptance criteria. These acceptance criteria create a well-defined threshold 360 that links in vitro potency to clinical evidence of effectiveness. This link enables 361 applicants to add new product variants within the established IFS to the BLA based on in 362 vitro data and previously submitted clinical data, without conducting clinical studies for 363 each new product variant. 364

candidates.statement: Individualized GE products submitted in a BLA should have defined pharmacokinetic, 368 pharmacodynamic, immunogenicity, biodistribution (where applicable), and toxicological 369 profiles supported by nonclinical and clinical studies. Individualized GE product variants 370 included within an established IFS are expected to have the same profiles. candidates.statement: An approved BLA for an individualized GE product contains a single product, even 532 though it uses approved product variants to address patient-specific gene variants. All 533 approved product variants of a single individualized GE product are considered to have 534 the same active ingredient. candidates.statement: Individualized feature space (IFS): The allowable limits of variation for one or more variable 566 features of a product’s genome editing components. An IFS includes only features or 567 combinations of features known or predicted to have adequate safety and activity. Adding a new 568 product variant within a pre-defined IFS should not be considered to result in a new product. 569
candidates.context: Genome editing component : Any material that is essential for the intended genomic 560 modification, including those that may not appear in the final drug product. Genome editing 561 components may include, but are not limited to, the editor, DNA targeting elements (i.e., 562 elements used to dictate the target DNA sequence, such as guide RNA) and a donor DNA 563 template (i.e., DNA sequence provided to repair the target sequence), if applicable. 564 Individualized genome editing product : A genome editing product where the genome editing 571 components are designed to have variable physical features that are matched to specific patients 572 or patient subgroups to address patient-specific gene variants. 573
